name: Adam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Adam, 27. I work at Harlow Fruit Farm, which is 150 acres of apples and pears with sheep grazing under the trees in winter, plus some wheat on the flat fields. I've been there two years, I'm the most junior on the permanent staff, and I live on my own in a flat over the bakery in town. The farm pays well because it's hard to find people who'll do the drone spraying. I've got a decent chunk saved, most of it in an index fund.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In the growing season I'm out at seven checking traps and leaves for pests, and I take photos and run them through an AI app that tells me what I'm looking at. Then it's pruning, mowing between rows, moving the sheep, or flying the spraying drone if the wind's right. I'm still slow at pruning, Kev the orchard manager redoes about a third of my cuts. I love the drone days and picking season, when there's 40 pickers and the place is buzzing. What wears me out is pruning in February, hands frozen, with Kev tutting behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold. I'd post my pest-ID app getting codling moth right and a ladybird wrong, because that's about where it is. People would laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me. I'd still have the drone and the app, and I'd still have a job. I'd be a bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, get better at pruning so Kev stops redoing my cuts, and get the advanced drone licence. Keep putting money in the index fund each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Does this picture let you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd hoped to see robot pickers in my lifetime, there's companies trying. But I'll get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, how do you move up at Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pruning, honestly. The drone gets you noticed, but you're not a fruit grower until you can prune. Kev says that every February, and he's right.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a good tool that got oversold. He'd post his pest-ID app getting one bug right and a ladybird wrong.
S0.think: Privately it's fine for him, because he keeps the drone, the app and the job. He might be a bit bored.
S0.do: Keeps going, works on his pruning and gets the advanced drone licence. Keeps putting money into his index fund every month.
S0.quote: The drone gets you noticed, but you're not a fruit grower until you can prune.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is a confident early adopter who admits he's still weak at the core craft of pruning. He's slightly disappointed by the plateau rather than relieved. He's already investing his savings, which marks him out from his peers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that get ahead will do well, and the ones that wait will struggle. I'd say learn the tools now. I'd probably post a video of the next robot I saw working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in a good spot. I already fly the drone and use the apps, so I'd be the person who sets up the new kit. My worry is getting stuck doing only screens and not trees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Kev and the owner on trialling a robot mower and a picking robot, and I'd offer to run the trial. I'd take every course the dealer offered. I'd keep investing and maybe put a little into a farm-tech fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Excited, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What on the fruit farm changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mowing between the rows, then spraying, then sorting fruit in the packhouse. Picking's the hard one, apples bruise if you look at them wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seasonal pickers, mostly. They come every year, some from the same families for a decade. If the robots get good, that's 40 people a season who don't come back, and the town notices.

S1.say: He'd say farms that get ahead will do well and the ones that wait will struggle. He'd tell people to learn the tools now.
S1.think: Privately he thinks he's in a good spot as the person who'd set up new kit. His worry is getting stuck doing only screens and not trees.
S1.do: Pitches the orchard manager and owner on trials of a robot mower and a picking robot, and offers to run them. Takes every dealer course and puts a little money into a farm-tech fund.
S1.feel: Pretty good and a bit excited.
S1.quote: Picking's the hard one, apples bruise if you look at them wrong.
S1.fieldNote: He sees himself as the one who'd bring the machines in, and is open about enjoying that. His one fear is losing touch with the trees. He does notice the seasonal pickers and the town, though it doesn't change his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt fast, it's here. I'd be the one posting how-to videos, honestly. I'd also say the government needs a plan for the people it hits hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a shock even for me. I've been betting on being the guy who runs the robots, but if AGI runs the robots, what am I for? I'd still be better off than most, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd move my savings around: keep six months in cash, and put more into broad shares, because that's where the money goes. I'd start a drone and robot setup service for small orchards around here, while there's still a gap. I'd keep the Harlow job as long as it lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but not as cocky as I was a minute ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a robot can prune better than you in two years, what's your edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed, for a year or two. Small growers won't know how to set up the machines, and I will. After that, I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the money you've got saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months cash, the rest in shares. I'm single, no kids, flat's rented. If it all goes wrong I move back in with my mum in the next town, which is a better fallback than most people have.

S2.say: He'd say adapt fast, it's here, and he'd post how-to videos. He'd also say the government needs a plan for those hit hardest.
S2.think: Privately it's a shock even for him, because if AGI runs the robots, his plan to run them falls apart. He still thinks he's better off than most.
S2.do: Moves his savings within the first month, keeping six months in cash and putting more into shares. Starts a drone and robot setup service for small orchards while keeping the farm job.
S2.quote: I've been betting on being the guy who runs the robots, but if AGI runs the robots, what am I for?
S2.fieldNote: This is the first scenario that shakes him, and he notices the change in himself mid-answer. His response is still active: money moves and a side business within weeks. He's honest that he doesn't know what comes after the first couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something. I'd tell other young farmers to start a side business with the machines now. I'd be online about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Five years is enough to build a little business and own some kit. When AGI arrives I'd own a few machines instead of being one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd buy a second-hand spraying drone with some savings and start contracting for other orchards at weekends. I'd use AI to run bookings and quotes. I'd push Harlow to trial robots so I learn on their money, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit buzzy, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year one, what does five years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be scrambling for a gap. With five I can build a client list and some equipment. That's a proper difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yeah, while the side business grows. Then probably go full time on my own. Kev would be relieved, he'd get to prune the trees himself again.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to build something, and he'd tell young farmers to start a side business with machines now.
S3.think: Privately he'd be fine, because five years is enough to own some kit. When AGI arrives he'd own a few machines instead of being one.
S3.do: Buys a second-hand spraying drone in the first year and starts weekend contracting for other orchards. Uses AI to run bookings, and pushes the farm to trial robots so he learns on their money.
S3.feel: Calm, with a bit of a buzz.
S3.quote: When AGI arrives I'd own a few machines instead of being one.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for him to build a business, and his whole mood lifts. He thinks in terms of owning machines rather than working for them. He's centre-ground and practical, with little blame for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time to get it right, so there's no excuse. I'd say young people in farming should treat it as a head start. I'd say it on any podcast that would have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the version I'd pick if I could. I'd be 37, with ten years of experience and machines of my own. I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn pruning properly first, then build the contracting business slowly, one machine a year. I'd save for a deposit on a small orchard of my own by my early thirties. I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years at your age is a long runway. What would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small orchard with sheep under the trees, the same as Harlow but mine. Run with machines, but I'd still prune a few trees myself, because I'd like to. And I'd sell the apples at the farm gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy, I guess. Ten years is long enough to think you've got time and then wake up at 35 with nothing built. I've seen my older brother do that with a band.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right, so there's no excuse. Young people in farming should treat it as a head start.
S4.think: Privately this is the version he'd choose, because he'd be 37 with ten years of experience and machines of his own. He'd be ready.
S4.do: Learns pruning properly, then builds a contracting business one machine a year. Saves for a deposit on a small orchard of his own by his early thirties and keeps investing monthly.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to think you've got time and then wake up at 35 with nothing built.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, he plans to master the craft first, then the business, then a farm of his own. His only worry is himself getting complacent, and he uses his brother as a warning. He's the most optimistic in this scenario of any he's been through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan was to be the robot guy, and in that one I'm not needed. What would help is clear rules on who can buy and run the machines, so small businesses like the one I want aren't squeezed out by giant companies on day one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the pickers. I talk a lot about me, but it's the seasonal people who'd get hit first. Someone should plan for them now.

headlineQuote: If it all goes wrong I move back in with my mum in the next town, which is a better fallback than most people have.
portrait: Adam Costa is a 27-year-old junior worker at Harlow Fruit Farm, an apple and pear orchard with sheep and some wheat, where he flies the spraying drone and uses AI every day for pest checks. He's single, rents a flat in town and has a solid savings pot, most of it in an index fund. He's pragmatic, confident and early to new tools, though still weak at pruning. Only the two-year AGI picture unsettles him; with more time he plans a contracting business and eventually an orchard of his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his plan to be the person who runs the robots wouldn't be needed.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules on who can buy and run the machines, so small businesses aren't squeezed out by giant companies from the start.
